lessons.title: What Is a Cell?
lessons.notes_html:
A cell is the basic unit of structure and function of living things. All living things are made up of cells. Cells are very small and cannot be seen with the naked eye, so we study them with a microscope. The word cell means a small room or a bounded space.

Both plant and animal cells have a cell membrane, cytoplasm and a nucleus. A group of similar cells together makes a tissue.

Who Gave the Name Cell?

  • The term cell was introduced in 1665 by the British scientist Robert Hooke.
  • He saw a thin slice of cork under a microscope.
  • He observed honeycomb-like structures and called them cells.

Key Points

  • A cell is the smallest unit of structure and function in living things.
  • Cells are seen with a microscope, not with the naked eye.
  • Robert Hooke introduced the term cell in 1665.

lessons.title: Parts of a Cell
lessons.notes_html:
Every cell has small parts called organelles. Each organelle does a special job for the cell.

Main Organelles

  • Cell membrane — made of lipids and protein. It controls the movement of materials into and out of the cell. It is partially permeable.
  • Cytoplasm — the jelly-like part where most cell activities take place.
  • Nucleus — the most prominent part. It controls all functions of the cell. It contains thread-like chromosomes, which are made of DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) and protein.
  • Mitochondria — the powerhouse of the cell. They release energy.
  • Vacuole — a sac-like structure. It stores salts, minerals and proteins and isolates waste products.
  • Ribosomes, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus and lysosomes — small organelles present in both plant and animal cells.

Key Points

  • The nucleus controls the cell; chromosomes are found in it.
  • Mitochondria are the powerhouse of the cell.
  • The cell membrane controls what enters and leaves the cell.

lessons.title: Plant Cell and Animal Cell
lessons.notes_html:
Plant and animal cells share many organelles, but they also differ in some important ways.

Similarities

Both have a cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus, lysosomes and vacuoles.

FeaturePlant cellAnimal cell
Cell wallPresent — outermost covering, mainly cellulose, hard and protectiveAbsent
ChloroplastPresent — contains green pigment chlorophyll for photosynthesisAbsent
VacuoleOne single large vacuole in the centreMany small vacuoles
NucleusPushed towards the cell membrane by the large vacuoleAlmost in the centre
CentriolesAbsentPresent near the nucleus

Key Points

  • Only plant cells have a cell wall and chloroplasts.
  • Chlorophyll in chloroplasts makes leaves green and helps in photosynthesis.
  • A plant cell has one large vacuole; an animal cell has many small ones.

lessons.title: Special Cells and Blood Cells
lessons.notes_html:
Cells of different shapes do different jobs — the shape fits the function.

Some Special Cells

  • Nerve cells (neurons) — long and branched fibres. They carry messages from the body to the brain and back.
  • Muscle cells — they contract and relax to produce movement.
  • Epithelium cells — flat and tightly packed layers covering the skin and inner linings. They protect, secrete and allow diffusion.
  • Xylem cells — long and tube-shaped. They carry water from roots to leaves.
  • Phloem cells — tubular. They transport food made in the leaves to all parts.

Cells in Blood

Blood is a liquid tissue. Its cells float in plasma, which distributes nutrients and removes wastes.

  • Red blood cells — disc-shaped. They contain haemoglobin, carry oxygen to the cells and remove carbon dioxide. They live about 120 days.
  • White blood cells — irregular in shape, with a nucleus and no haemoglobin. They are part of the immune system and fight and kill germs.
  • Platelets — the smallest blood cells, without a nucleus. They help the blood to clot and stop bleeding.

Key Points

  • Long nerve cells carry messages; muscle cells move the body.
  • Red cells carry oxygen, white cells fight germs, platelets stop bleeding.

lessons.title: From Cells to Organ Systems
lessons.notes_html:
Living bodies are organized in levels. Each level is built from the level below it.

The Levels

  • Cell — the basic unit of living things.
  • Tissue — a group of similar cells working together.
  • Organ — a part made of tissues that does a special job.
  • Organ system — a group of organs that work together for one function.

Organization in Plants

Plant organs are root, stem, leaves, flower and fruit. The root system (root and its branches) absorbs water and minerals from the soil. The shoot system (stem, branches, leaves and flowers) is the above-ground part and gives support. The vascular system of xylem and phloem transports water and food.

Organization in Humans

Human organs include the heart, lungs, kidneys, liver, eyes, brain, stomach and intestines. The digestive system digests food, the respiratory system takes in oxygen and removes carbon dioxide, the circulatory system transports blood, and the nervous system controls movement, sensation and thinking. The human body has 11 major organ systems.

Key Points

  • Cell, then tissue, then organ, then organ system.
  • Plants have a root system and a shoot system.
  • Many organ systems work together to keep the body alive.

lessons.title: Reproduction: Sexual and Asexual
lessons.notes_html:
Reproduction is the biological process by which organisms produce offspring of their own kind. It is a basic property of all living things. It ensures the survival of living organisms and the continuation of plant species.

FeatureSexual reproductionAsexual reproduction
GametesMale and female gametes (sperms and eggs) fuseNo fusion of gametes
ParentsTwo parentsOnly one parent
OffspringHave characters of both parents; not identicalIdentical to the parent
Parts usedFlowers, fruits and seedsVegetative parts like bulbs, tubers and runners

The male gamete is called sperm and the female gamete is called egg.

Key Points

  • Reproduction produces offspring of the same kind.
  • Sexual reproduction needs two parents and fusion of gametes.
  • Asexual reproduction needs one parent and gives identical offspring.

lessons.title: Parts of a Flower
lessons.notes_html:
The flower is the reproductive part of a plant. It has four main parts: sepals, petals, stamens and carpels.

The Four Parts

  • Sepals — green, leaf-like structures. They protect the flower in the bud stage.
  • Petals — coloured, showy and attractive. They attract birds and insects for pollination.
  • Stamen — the male part. It has two parts: the anther, the swollen part where pollen grains are formed, and the filament, a long stalk-like structure.
  • Carpel — the female part. It has three parts: the stigma at the top, which receives pollen grains; the style, a long tube that passes pollen to the ovary; and the ovary, the swollen basal part containing the ovule, which bears the egg.

Key Points

  • Sepals protect the bud; petals attract pollinators.
  • Stamen is the male part; carpel is the female part.
  • Pollen forms in the anther; the egg is in the ovule inside the ovary.

lessons.title: Pollination and Fertilization
lessons.notes_html:
Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma. It is the first step of sexual reproduction in flowering plants.

Two Types of Pollination

  • Self-pollination — pollen reaches the stigma of the same flower, or of another flower on the same plant. Examples: pea, tomato and cotton.
  • Cross-pollination — pollen reaches the stigma of a flower on another plant of the same species. Examples: maize, rose and papaya.

Fertilization

After pollination, a pollen tube grows and enters the ovary. It releases its sperms into the ovule. One sperm fuses with the egg and forms a zygote. This fusion is called fertilization.

Key Points

  • Pollination moves pollen from anther to stigma.
  • Self-pollination stays on one plant; cross-pollination goes to another plant.
  • Fertilization forms a zygote inside the ovule.

lessons.title: Seeds, Fruits and Germination
lessons.notes_html:
After fertilization, the flower changes into seeds and fruit, and the seeds grow into new plants.

Seed and Fruit Formation

  • The zygote develops into an embryo.
  • The ovule containing the embryo forms a seed.
  • The ovary grows large and develops into a fruit, which protects the seeds.
  • The embryo gradually develops into cotyledons, plumule and radicle.

Seed Dispersal and Germination

Seeds are dispersed by wind, animals or water, so new plants can grow away from the parent. Fully mature seeds sown in soil germinate when favourable conditions like moisture and suitable temperature are available. A seedling emerges and grows into a new plant. This is called seed germination.

Key Points

  • Ovule becomes seed; ovary becomes fruit.
  • Seeds spread by wind, animals and water.
  • Germination needs moisture and a suitable temperature.

lessons.title: Natural Vegetative Propagation
lessons.notes_html:
In vegetative propagation, new plants grow from the vegetative parts of the parent plant — roots, stem, leaves and branches. No gametes fuse, so the new plants are identical to the parent. The vegetative parts of a plant are roots, stem, leaves and branches; the flower is its reproductive part.

Natural Methods

  • Bulb — an underground stem with thick, food-storing leaves. It reproduces through buds — a bud is an outgrowth in the centre of the bulb, and when buried in soil a new plant grows from it. Examples: onion, tulip, daffodil.
  • Tuber — an underground thick stem. Its buds are called eyes. Pieces of potato having eyes, buried in soil, grow into new plants.
  • Runner — a special stem that spreads over the ground horizontally. It has nodes where buds are present, and new plants grow from these buds. Examples: grasses and strawberry.

Bulb or Tuber?

Both are underground stems. A bulb stores food in thick leaves around a central bud, while a tuber is itself a thickened stem with eyes as buds.

Key Points

  • Natural propagation happens by itself through bulbs, tubers and runners.
  • A bulb reproduces through buds; a tuber through its eyes.
  • Runners grow new plants from buds at their nodes.

lessons.title: Artificial Vegetative Propagation
lessons.notes_html:
Artificial vegetative propagation is practised by humans. It has been used for hundreds of years to grow plants with desired traits.

Artificial Methods

  • Cutting — a stem piece with buds is cut and planted in soil. Buds on the underground part grow into roots; buds on the aerial part grow into stem and leaves. Examples: rose, grapes, sugar cane.
  • Grafting — a cut piece of a plant, the scion, is joined with another plant, the stock, so both grow as a single plant.
  • Layering — a stem is buried in soil without cutting it off; roots grow, then it is separated.
  • Budding — a bud from one plant is grafted onto the stem of another plant.

Advantages

Many plants grow rapidly with desired traits, all year round. Rare and endangered species can be protected, yield and quality improve, disease and drought resistant varieties can be developed, and seedless fruits like oranges and grapes can be produced. Grafting and budding are used for mangoes and many woody and nursery plants.

Key Points

  • Cutting, grafting, layering and budding are artificial methods.
  • In grafting, the scion is joined to the stock.
  • Artificial propagation gives more, better and even seedless fruits.

lessons.title: Diet and Balanced Diet
lessons.notes_html:
The food and drinks we consume daily are called our diet. A balanced diet is a diet that contains all the essential nutrients a person needs for living a healthy life, in precise proportions.

What a Balanced Diet Contains

  • A good proportion of carbohydrates and proteins.
  • A small amount of fats.
  • Minerals and vitamins, which are essential for health.
  • Water and fibre as well.

On the basis of nutrients, foods are classified into five major groups: carbohydrates, proteins, fats and oils, vitamins, and minerals.

A diet that lacks the essential components needed for normal functioning is an unbalanced diet. It causes nutritional deficiency disorders.

Key Points

  • A balanced diet has all nutrients in precise proportions.
  • Carbohydrates and proteins in good proportion; fats in small amount.
  • An unbalanced diet causes deficiency disorders.

lessons.title: Carbohydrates and Fats: Energy Foods
lessons.notes_html:
Carbohydrates are the main and primary source of energy for our body. They act as fuel for the body.

Carbohydrates

  • They include glucose, sugar and starch, and are made up of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.
  • We get them from bread, rice, cereals, milk, honey, fruits and vegetables.
  • They are a quick source of energy. They are absorbed in the wall of the small intestine and reach every cell through blood.
  • Extra carbohydrates are stored in the liver as glycogen.
  • Our brain almost completely depends on carbohydrates for energy.
  • Their deficiency causes fatigue, weakness, low weight and constipation.

Fats

  • Fats are a rich source of energy: they provide twice the energy of carbohydrates.
  • They are part of the cell membrane, help make and regulate hormones, and help absorb vitamins A, D, E and K.
  • Animal sources: meat, poultry, fish, eggs, butter, ghee and oil. Plant sources: olive oil, palm oil, canola oil and coconut oil.
  • Plant fats are considered good for health. Too much animal fat may cause heart diseases and obesity, so a balanced diet has only a small amount of fats.

Key Points

  • Carbohydrates are the primary, quick source of energy.
  • Fats give twice the energy of carbohydrates.
  • Vitamins A, D, E and K need fat to be absorbed.

lessons.title: Proteins, Water and Fibre
lessons.notes_html:
Proteins are large molecules made up of amino acids. There are about 20 different types of amino acids. On average, protein makes up about 16% of a person's body weight.

Why We Need Proteins

  • They build our body tissues while we are growing.
  • They build and repair body tissues.
  • Enzymes and hormones are built up of protein.
  • Proteins are part of antibodies, which fight disease-causing bacteria.
  • Protein deficiency causes the disorders kwashiorkor and marasmus.

Sources of Protein

  • Animal sources: meat (chicken, mutton, beef, fish), eggs, milk, cheese and yogurt.
  • Plant sources: beans, pulses, nuts, seeds, peas, legumes and oats.

Water is also an essential part of a balanced diet. About 55–60% of our body is water. A balanced diet also includes fibre, which helps the digestive system work well.

Key Points

  • Proteins are made of amino acids and build and repair the body.
  • Enzymes, hormones and antibodies are made of protein.
  • About 55–60% of our body is water.

lessons.title: Vitamins, Minerals and Deficiency Disorders
lessons.notes_html:
Our body needs vitamins and minerals in small amounts. Missing any of them causes a deficiency disorder.

NutrientSource / RoleDeficiency causes
Vitamin ACarrot and other foodsPoor vision, night blindness
Vitamin CCitrus fruitsBleeding gums (scurvy)
Vitamin DLiver, egg, fish, dairy; skin makes it in sunlightWeak, soft bones (rickets)
CalciumMakes bones and teeth strongWeak bones
IronPart of haemoglobinAnaemia (lack of red blood cells)
IodineNeeded by the thyroid glandGoiter (swelling in the neck)

Dietary minerals are elements like calcium, phosphorus, magnesium, potassium, iron, sodium, iodine and zinc. They keep bones and teeth strong, regulate body fluids and support the immune system. They are found in milk, meat, cereals, vegetables, fruits, egg and fish.

Key Points

  • Iron deficiency causes anaemia; iodine deficiency causes goiter.
  • Vitamin C deficiency causes bleeding gums; vitamin D deficiency weakens bones.
  • A balanced diet prevents all deficiency disorders.

lessons.title: Food Pyramid and Diet for Every Age
lessons.notes_html:
The food pyramid is a conical guide chart for a balanced diet. Its wide base shows the foods we can take the most; its top shows the foods we should take the least.

The Food Pyramid

  • Bread, cereals and potatoes — 4 servings (base).
  • Fruit and vegetables — 2–4 servings.
  • Milk, cheese and dairy — 3 servings.
  • Meat, fish and alternatives — 2 small servings.
  • Fats, oils and confectionery — sparingly, at the top.

Diet Changes with Age

  • Children (1–12 years) — breast feeding up to 18 months; then fruits, grains, vegetables, meat (chicken, fish), yogurt and milk.
  • Adults (13–19 years) — calcium-rich and iron-rich food, vitamin D rich food (fish, dairy), sunlight, fruits, vegetables and meat.
  • Young adults (20–39 years) — whole grains, calcium, iron and vitamin D rich products, vegetables, fruits, meat, dry fruits and yogurt.
  • Old age (40–60 years) — grains (brown rice, wheat), leafy vegetables, fruits, lean protein (chicken, fish), low fat milk and nuts.

Fitness depends on a balanced diet and regular exercise — we are what we eat.

Key Points

  • The pyramid base is taken most; the top is taken least.
  • Growing children need milk and growth foods; old age needs lean protein and low fat milk.
  • Balanced diet plus regular exercise keeps us fit.

lessons.title: Digestion: Physical and Chemical
lessons.notes_html:
Digestion is the process by which the body breaks down food into smaller, soluble and diffusible particles. These particles can be absorbed into the blood and used for energy, growth and maintenance of the body. Food pieces are too large to be absorbed, so they must first be broken down.

Two Types of Digestion

  • Physical digestion — the mechanical breakdown of food into smaller particles, so enzymes can act on it easily. It starts in the mouth, where teeth break food into small pieces, and continues in the stomach and small intestine.
  • Chemical digestion — enzymes break food particles into smaller and simpler components that can be absorbed easily.

What Are Enzymes?

Enzymes are biological molecules made of protein. They speed up chemical reactions in the body but themselves remain unchanged. For example, amylases digest starch, lipases digest fat, and proteases digest proteins.

Key Points

  • Digestion breaks food into smaller soluble molecules.
  • Physical digestion is mechanical; chemical digestion is done by enzymes.
  • Enzymes speed up reactions and remain unchanged.

lessons.title: Mouth, Esophagus and Stomach
lessons.notes_html:
The digestive system consists of the alimentary canal and the digestive glands. The canal is a long tube, about 30 feet long, from mouth to anus. Food takes about 24 hours to pass through it. Kidneys are not part of it.

Mouth and Esophagus

  • In the oral cavity, teeth mechanically digest food. The tongue, with taste buds, mixes saliva with food to make a soft bolus. Saliva contains salivary amylase, which breaks carbohydrates into simpler sugars.
  • The pharynx is a common path for food and air.
  • The esophagus is a short, narrow, muscular tube. It pushes food balls into the stomach by peristalsis — wave-like muscle contractions. No digestion takes place in it.

Stomach

The stomach is a muscular, J-shaped sac in the upper abdomen, with valves at both ends. Its wall secretes gastric juice with hydrochloric acid and the enzyme pepsin. The acid kills bacteria and pepsin digests protein. Food stays inside for 1 to 6 hours.

Key Points

  • Digestion starts in the mouth; the esophagus only transports food.
  • Peristalsis pushes food through the esophagus.
  • Gastric juice has hydrochloric acid and pepsin, which digests protein.

lessons.title: Small Intestine and Absorption
lessons.notes_html:
The small intestine is a long, coiled, muscular tube between the stomach and the large intestine. It is about 6 metres long — the longest part of the digestive system — and most digestion and absorption happen here.

Its Three Parts

  • Duodenum — the first part. Bile from the gall bladder and pancreatic juice from the pancreas are poured into it.
  • Jejunum — the second part. It absorbs digested nutrients.
  • Ileum — the third part. It also absorbs nutrients and passes undigested waste to the large intestine.

How Absorption Happens

The wall of the small intestine has small finger-like projections called villi. They contain blood vessels. Digested, diffusible nutrients are absorbed through the villi into the blood, and blood then carries them to all parts of the body. About 90% of nutrient absorption takes place in the small intestine. Pancreatic juice is rich in enzymes — amylase, lipase (which digests fat into fatty acids and glycerol) and trypsin — which complete the digestion of food.

Key Points

  • Duodenum, jejunum and ileum are the three parts of the small intestine.
  • Villi absorb nutrients into the blood.
  • About 90% of absorption happens in the small intestine.

lessons.title: Large Intestine and Digestive Glands
lessons.notes_html:
After the small intestine, the remaining material enters the large intestine, also called the colon. It is the terminal part of the canal, about 1.5 m long.

Large Intestine and Rectum

  • The walls of the large intestine absorb water and minerals into the blood.
  • The remaining waste moves into the rectum and is stored there for 12 to 24 hours.
  • Muscles in the rectum wall control the release of faeces through the anus. This is called egestion or defecation.

Jobs of the Digestive Parts

JobOrgan or part
Chews foodTeeth (in the mouth)
Releases salivaSalivary glands
Releases gastric juiceStomach
Produces bileLiver (bile is stored in the gall bladder)
Produces enzymesPancreas
Absorbs nutrientsSmall intestine
Absorbs water and saltsLarge intestine
Stores faecesRectum

Key Points

  • The large intestine absorbs water and minerals, not nutrients.
  • The liver produces bile; the gall bladder only stores it.
  • Waste is stored in the rectum before egestion.

lessons.title: Digestive Disorders
lessons.notes_html:
When the digestive system does not work properly, disorders appear. The common digestive disorders are diarrhoea, constipation, ulcers and indigestion.

Diarrhoea

  • Passing loose stool more than 3 times a day, with abdominal cramps, bloating, nausea and sometimes vomiting.
  • It is caused by irritation of the digestive tract by a virus or bacteria, by some medicine, or by rotten food.
  • Water and nutrients are not absorbed, so the patient loses water — dehydration.
  • The patient must take plenty of boiled water with oral rehydration salt (ORS), fresh fruits and properly cooked vegetables.

Constipation

  • The opposite of diarrhoea: infrequent bowel movements with dry, hard stool that is difficult to pass out.
  • It occurs due to slow peristalsis because of poor diet, dehydration or physical inactivity. More water is absorbed by the large intestine, so the stool becomes dry and hard.
  • It is relieved by plenty of water, fibre-rich food like fruits and vegetables, and physical activity and exercise.

Symptoms of an ulcer are also studied in this unit as a digestive disorder.

Key Points

  • Diarrhoea means loose stool and dehydration; ORS replaces lost water and minerals.
  • Constipation means dry, hard stool due to slow peristalsis.
  • Water, fibre and exercise prevent constipation.

lessons.title: Particle Theory of Matter
lessons.notes_html:
All matter is made of tiny particles. Scientists developed the particle theory of matter to explain the nature of matter.

Main Points of the Theory

  • All matter is composed of tiny particles called atoms and molecules.
  • The particles are in continuous motion.
  • There is space between the particles.
  • The particles have a force of attraction among them.
  • Heat affects the movement of particles — heat makes the particles move faster.

Evidence for the Theory

  • An inflated balloon goes down after a while, because tiny air particles escape through millions of tiny holes in it.
  • Pressing air in a syringe becomes harder and harder because of the air pressure inside.
  • Sugar dissolves in water and disappears, because sugar particles move into the empty spaces between water particles.
  • On boiling salt water, water changes into steam and salt is left behind.

Key Points

  • Matter is made of atoms and molecules in continuous motion.
  • There are spaces and attractive forces between particles.
  • Heat makes particles move faster.

lessons.title: Solids, Liquids and Gases
lessons.notes_html:
Matter exists in three physical states: solid, liquid and gas. The states differ because their particles are arranged differently.

FeatureSolidLiquidGas
ParticlesTightly packed in a regular pattern called a crystal latticeClose, but not in orderFar apart, with large empty spaces
MovementLocked in place; only vibrateFree to moveFree to move in any direction; collide with each other and the walls
Force of attractionStrongestWeaker than solidsWeakest
Shape and volumeDefinite shape and volumeDefinite volume, no definite shapeNo fixed shape or volume
FlowDoes not flowFlows and takes the shape of its containerFlows and fills any available space
ExamplesIron, copper, sugar, saltWater, oil, vinegar, mercuryAir, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, helium

Mercury is the only metal on Earth that is liquid at room temperature.

Key Points

  • Solids have definite shape and volume; liquids have definite volume only.
  • Gas particles have the highest kinetic energy and the weakest attraction.
  • Mercury is a liquid metal.

lessons.title: Melting, Freezing and Boiling
lessons.notes_html:
Heating and cooling change the state of matter, because they change the movement of particles.

Melting and Freezing

  • Melting — the conversion of a solid into a liquid at a specific temperature, called the melting point.
  • Freezing — the conversion of a liquid into a solid upon cooling at a specific temperature, called the freezing point. On cooling, particles move slowly and get fixed positions.
  • The freezing point and melting point of water are both 0°C.

Boiling

  • Boiling is the conversion of a liquid into a gas by heating at a specific temperature, the boiling point.
  • On heating, particles gain energy and move faster, so the attractive forces weaken and the liquid changes into gas.
  • The boiling point of water is 100°C.

Key Points

  • Cooling a liquid freezes it into a solid.
  • Water freezes and melts at 0°C and boils at 100°C.
  • Boiling happens at one fixed temperature.

lessons.title: Evaporation, Condensation and Sublimation
lessons.notes_html:
Some changes of state happen without melting or boiling in the usual way.

Evaporation

  • Evaporation is the escaping of liquid particles from the surface of an open container.
  • It takes place at all temperatures. Particles absorb heat from the atmosphere and escape.
  • Its rate increases when the temperature increases — water evaporates faster in hot summer than in cold winter.
  • So boiling is a bulk change at a fixed temperature, while evaporation is a surface change at all temperatures.

Condensation

Condensation is the conversion of a gas into a liquid upon cooling. On cooling, the particles come close together and change into liquid — for example, moisture in warm air condensing on a cold glass.

Sublimation

Sublimation is the conversion of a solid directly into a gas, without passing through the liquid state. Examples: iodine, ammonium chloride, naphthalene and dry ice (solid carbon dioxide). Dry ice is used to keep materials cold and dry.

Key Points

  • Evaporation is a surface change at all temperatures.
  • Condensation changes gas into liquid on cooling.
  • Sublimation changes solid directly into gas, as in dry ice.

lessons.title: Diffusion
lessons.notes_html:
Diffusion is the movement of particles from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration.

Diffusion and Particle Theory

  • Particles are in continuous motion, so they spread out by themselves.
  • Gas particles move faster than liquid particles, so diffusion takes place in liquids and gases, but not in solids — solid particles cannot move from their place.
  • Gases show more diffusion than liquids.
  • Large and heavy particles diffuse slowly; small and light particles diffuse faster.
  • An increase in temperature makes particles move faster, so the rate of diffusion increases.

Example

A few drops of ink in a beaker of water first form a small dark droplet. Then the ink gradually spreads and diffuses, and after about 1 hour the entire solution becomes a uniform pale colour.

Key Points

  • Diffusion moves particles from higher to lower concentration.
  • It happens in liquids and gases, fastest in gases.
  • Heat and small particle size increase the rate of diffusion.

lessons.title: Atoms and Subatomic Particles
lessons.notes_html:
An atom is the smallest particle of matter that can take part in a chemical reaction and show the chemical properties of the element. It is the building block of matter. The word atom is Greek for indivisible.

Structure of an Atom

  • Nucleus — the centre of the atom. It contains protons and neutrons.
  • Protons — positively charged particles in the nucleus.
  • Neutrons — particles in the nucleus with no electrical charge; they are neutral.
  • Electrons — negatively charged particles revolving around the nucleus in different orbits.

The number of electrons and protons in an atom are equal, so an atom is a neutral particle. About 99.9% of the volume of an atom is empty, because the electrons orbit far away from the nucleus. The hydrogen atom is the smallest atom: it has one proton, one electron and no neutron.

Key Points

  • Protons and neutrons are in the nucleus; electrons revolve around it.
  • Protons are positive, electrons negative, neutrons neutral.
  • Equal protons and electrons make an atom neutral.

lessons.title: Atomic Number, Mass Number and Molecules
lessons.notes_html:
Two numbers describe every atom: its atomic number and its mass number.

Atomic Number and Mass Number

  • Atomic number (Z) — the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom. It is the identity of an element and is unique to each element. Hydrogen has atomic number 1 and helium has 2.
  • Mass number (A) — the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus: mass number = atomic number + number of neutrons.

Molecules

A molecule is a group of two or more atoms joined chemically. Atoms of most elements are unstable and cannot exist alone, so they join to form molecules. Only the atoms of noble gases (helium, neon, argon) are stable and exist independently.

  • Monoatomic — one atom, e.g. helium (He), neon (Ne), argon (Ar).
  • Diatomic — two atoms, e.g. oxygen (O2) and hydrogen (H2).
  • Triatomic — three atoms, e.g. ozone (O3) and water (H2O).

Key Points

  • Atomic number = number of protons; mass number = protons + neutrons.
  • A molecule is two or more atoms joined chemically.
  • Ozone is triatomic: three oxygen atoms.

lessons.title: Elements and the Periodic Table
lessons.notes_html:
An element is a substance made up of only one type of atoms, all with the same number of protons. It cannot be broken down into simpler substances. Examples: hydrogen, oxygen, carbon, nitrogen.

Symbols and the Periodic Table

Each element has a symbol — a one or two letter abbreviation; the first letter is capital and the second, if any, is small. The periodic table arranges all elements by increasing atomic number. Dmitri Mendeleev invented the modern periodic table. So far 118 elements are known; 92 occur naturally and the rest are synthesized.

No.ElementSymbolProtons
1HydrogenH1
2HeliumHe2
3LithiumLi3
4BerylliumBe4
5BoronB5
6CarbonC6
7NitrogenN7
8OxygenO8
9FluorineF9
10NeonNe10

Key Points

  • An element has only one type of atoms.
  • There are 118 known elements; 92 are natural.
  • Carbon has 6 protons and oxygen has 8 protons.

lessons.title: Metals, Non-metals and Metalloids
lessons.notes_html:
Elements are classified into three groups by their properties: metals, non-metals and metalloids.

PropertyMetalsNon-metals
State and weightHard, solid and heavyUsually gases, or solids that melt easily
AppearanceShiny when polishedDull
Boiling pointHigh; difficult to meltLow; melt easily
ConductorsGood conductors of heat and electricityPoor conductors of heat and electricity

Metalloids have properties of both metals and non-metals. Boron, silicon, arsenic and antimony are metalloids. Among the first 10 elements, only lithium and beryllium are metals; the others are non-metals.

Some Special Forms

  • Carbon exists in three forms: coal, graphite and diamond.
  • Graphite is a black, soft, slippery solid used in lead pencils.
  • Diamond is colourless, transparent and the hardest solid; used in jewelry and cutting tools.
  • Neon is a non-reactive noble gas. It glows orange when electricity passes through it, so it is used in advertising signs.

Key Points

  • Metals are shiny and good conductors; non-metals are dull and poor conductors.
  • Metalloids show properties of both groups.
  • Graphite and diamond are both forms of carbon.

lessons.title: Compounds
lessons.notes_html:
A compound is a pure substance of two or more kinds of elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio. It can be broken down only by chemical means, and its properties differ from its elements.

Element or Compound?

  • An element has one type of atoms, cannot be broken down, and is represented by a symbol, e.g. H, O, C, Na, Cl.
  • A compound has two or more different elements, can be broken down chemically, and is represented by a chemical formula, e.g. H2O, CO2, NaCl.
  • A molecule of the same element, like O2, is not a compound. Water (H2O) is both a molecule and a compound: two elements and three atoms.

Word Equations

  • Sodium + chlorine gives sodium chloride (NaCl) — common table salt.
  • Carbon + hydrogen gives methane (CH4).
  • Carbon + hydrogen + oxygen gives glucose (C6H12O6).
  • Nitrogen + hydrogen gives ammonia (NH3).

Sodium is a reactive metal and chlorine a toxic gas, yet together they form harmless table salt. Hydrogen is flammable and oxygen helps burning, yet their water extinguishes fire.

Key Points

  • A compound joins different elements in a fixed ratio.
  • Water is H2O, ammonia NH3, glucose C6H12O6.
  • A compound has new properties, unlike its elements.

lessons.title: What Is a Mixture?
lessons.notes_html:
A mixture is the physical combination of two or more substances. The substances are gathered physically, not chemically combined, so each substance keeps its own properties. A mixture can be separated easily by physical means. Air, tea, coffee and juice are all mixtures.

Mixture or Pure Substance?

  • A mixture is an impure substance. It contains different types of particles.
  • Pure substances — elements and compounds — are made of the same type of particles and have uniform composition.

Mixture vs Compound

  • In a mixture, substances are only physically combined, keep their own properties, and can be separated by physical means. Its composition is not fixed.
  • In a compound, elements are chemically joined in a fixed ratio. The compound has different properties from its elements and can be broken down only by chemical means.
  • An element is made of one kind of atoms, e.g. hydrogen, oxygen, carbon. Air is 78% nitrogen, the most abundant gas in it.

Key Points

  • A mixture is a physical combination, separable by physical means.
  • Mixtures are impure; elements and compounds are pure.
  • Parts of a mixture keep their own properties.

lessons.title: Homogeneous and Heterogeneous Mixtures
lessons.notes_html:
Mixtures are of two main types, depending on whether their composition is the same throughout.

The Two Types

  • Homogeneous mixture — has uniform composition and properties throughout the sample. Examples: salt solution, sugar solution, tea, coffee, milk, sea water, blood and air.
  • Heterogeneous mixture — has non-uniform composition and properties, so its parts can be seen separately. Examples: soil, salad and burger.

Alloys

An alloy is a homogeneous mixture of two or more elements in which one element must be a metal. Alloys are made by mixing the metals in molten form and letting them cool. Examples: stainless steel (iron with chromium), brass, bronze and red gold (gold with copper). Stainless steel is corrosion (rust) resistant and more durable, so it is used for cutlery. Plain iron is not an alloy.

Key Points

  • Homogeneous means uniform throughout; heterogeneous means non-uniform.
  • Tea and air are homogeneous; salad and soil are heterogeneous.
  • Steel, brass, bronze and red gold are alloys.

lessons.title: Solutions: Solute, Solvent and Water
lessons.notes_html:
A solution is a homogeneous mixture with two components: the solute and the solvent.

The Two Components

  • Solute — the part present in the lesser (smaller) quantity, e.g. sugar in sugar solution.
  • Solvent — the liquid part present in the greater quantity, e.g. water in sugar solution.

Water — the Universal Solvent

Water is called the universal solvent because most substances dissolve in it. A solution in which water is the solvent is called an aqueous solution — for example, sugar or salt dissolved in water.

Salt solution and sugar solution are common examples. In each one, water is the solvent and the dissolved substance is the solute.

Key Points

  • The solute is the smaller part; the solvent is the larger, liquid part.
  • Water is the universal solvent.
  • A water-based solution is an aqueous solution.

lessons.title: Separating Mixtures I: Filtration and Decantation
lessons.notes_html:
Because the parts of a mixture are only physically combined, simple physical methods can separate them.

Filtration

  • Filtration separates a suspended solid from a liquid using filter paper.
  • The mixture is poured through filter paper fitted in a funnel.
  • The liquid that passes through into the beaker is called the filtrate.
  • The solid trapped on the filter paper is called the residue.
  • Example: sand particles are separated from water this way — water passes through and sand stays on the paper.

Decantation

Decantation separates two liquids that do not mix, by pouring off the top layer. The less dense liquid floats on the denser one — as oil floats on water. Example: petrol and water are separated by decantation, because petrol floats on water and its top layer can be poured off.

Key Points

  • Filtration gives a filtrate (liquid) and a residue (solid).
  • Decantation pours off the floating top layer.
  • Oil and petrol float on water because they are less dense.

lessons.title: Separating Mixtures II: Evaporation and Distillation
lessons.notes_html:
Two more separation methods use heating: evaporation and distillation.

Evaporation

  • Evaporation separates a dissolved solid from a liquid.
  • The solution is heated, the liquid evaporates, and the pure solid is left behind.
  • Example: sugar is recovered from sugar and water by evaporation — the water evaporates and the sugar remains.

Distillation

  • Distillation separates liquids that have different boiling points — the boiling points of two liquids cannot be the same.
  • On heating, the liquid with the lower boiling point evaporates first. It is then condensed and collected separately, while the other liquid is left behind.
  • The unit demonstrates it with salt solution: the water evaporates and is collected, and the salt is left behind in the flask.

Choosing the Right Method

  • Solid suspended in liquid — filtration.
  • Two unmixed liquids — decantation.
  • Dissolved solid in liquid — evaporation.
  • Liquids with different boiling points — distillation.

Key Points

  • Evaporation leaves the dissolved solid behind.
  • Distillation uses different boiling points, then condenses the vapour.
  • Each mixture has a suitable physical separation method.

lessons.title: Energy and Its Unit
lessons.notes_html:
Energy is the ability to do work. All living things and machines need energy to do work — for cooking food, playing, running vehicles, glowing a bulb, cooling and heating our homes and running electronic devices. Plants also need energy for growth and for preparing their food from sunlight.

Energy Is a Physical Quantity

  • Physical quantities are quantities that can be measured.
  • Distance is measured in metres or kilometres, mass in grams or kilograms, and volume of liquids in litres or millilitres.
  • Energy is also a physical quantity. The unit used for the measurement of energy is the joule.
  • Examples: the kinetic energy of a moving ball, the potential energy of water stored behind a dam, and the thermal energy of a hot object — all expressed in joules.

Key Points

  • Energy is the ability to do work.
  • Energy can be measured, so it is a physical quantity.
  • The unit of energy is the joule.

lessons.title: Potential and Kinetic Energy
lessons.notes_html:
Energy due to position and energy due to motion are the two basic forms of energy.

The Two Forms

  • Potential energy — the energy stored in an object due to its position. Examples: a stone raised to a height, and water stored behind a dam.
  • Elastic potential energy — energy stored when an object is stretched or compressed. A stretched rubber band has elastic potential energy; when released, it changes into kinetic energy.
  • Kinetic energy — the energy due to the motion of an object. Examples: a moving ball, flowing water and a flying aeroplane.

Potential and kinetic energy are interconvertible: potential energy can change into kinetic energy and back again. In a roller coaster, cars gain potential energy as they climb and change it into kinetic energy as they come down. In a bouncing ball, gravitational potential energy changes into kinetic energy as it falls; on hitting the ground, part of it changes into elastic potential, sound and heat energy.

Key Points

  • Potential energy is due to position; kinetic energy is due to motion.
  • A stretched rubber band stores elastic potential energy.
  • The two forms keep changing into each other.

lessons.title: Conservation of Energy and Converters
lessons.notes_html:
The law of conservation of energy states that energy can neither be created nor destroyed. It can only be changed from one form to another, so the total energy remains constant.

Energy Converters

Energy converters are devices or processes which convert one form of energy into another form.

ConverterEnergy change
Plant (tree)Solar (light) energy into chemical energy stored in food
Solar panelLight energy into electrical energy
Car engineChemical energy of fuel into heat, then kinetic energy
TelevisionElectrical energy into sound and light energy
Washing machineElectrical energy into kinetic energy and sound energy
Electric kettleElectrical energy into thermal (heat) energy
CatapultElastic potential energy into kinetic energy
BatsmanChemical energy from food into kinetic energy

Sound energy is produced by vibrations — a bell, a drum, a loudspeaker or a car horn. Food stores chemical energy made by plants from solar energy.

Key Points

  • Energy is never created or destroyed; it only changes form.
  • A solar panel changes light into electrical energy.
  • Sound energy is produced by vibrations.

lessons.title: Renewable Energy Resources
lessons.notes_html:
Renewable sources of energy are permanent and recoverable. They have an endless supply, are cheap and free of cost, and are environment friendly — they produce no pollution.

Renewable Sources

  • Solar energy — from the sun.
  • Flowing water — hydroelectric power.
  • Wind energy.
  • Energy from plants and biogas energy.

Solar Energy

Solar energy is the energy obtained from the sun in the form of heat and light. It is the major source of energy on Earth and sustains life. Plants use it to make their food, changing it into chemical energy. Nowadays solar panels use it to produce electricity for devices such as solar fans and solar bulbs: a small solar panel connected to a DC fan makes the fan rotate in direct sunlight. A solar water heater uses copper tubing and an insulated tank to heat and store water with sunlight. Solar energy is free, clean and everlasting.

Key Points

  • Sun, flowing water, wind, plants and biogas are renewable.
  • Renewable energy is cheap, endless and pollution-free.
  • Plants change solar energy into chemical energy.

lessons.title: Non-renewable Resources and Saving Energy
lessons.notes_html:
Non-renewable sources of energy cannot be replaced once they are used up. Their supply is limited.

FeatureRenewableNon-renewable
SupplyEndless, recoverableLimited; cannot be recovered once depleted
CostCheap and free of costCostly
EnvironmentFriendly; no pollutionBurning causes air pollution
ExamplesSun, flowing water, wind, plants, biogasCoal, oil, natural gas

Coal, oil and natural gas are called fossil fuels. They were formed over millions of years from dead organisms. Burning them releases carbon dioxide, which raises the Earth's temperature — global warming. Energy obtained from plants is renewable, while coal is non-renewable. We should reduce energy consumption at home and school and prefer cheap, renewable and environment-friendly sources like the sun, wind, flowing water and biogas.

Key Points

  • Fossil fuels took millions of years to form and will finish one day.
  • Burning fossil fuels pollutes air and causes global warming.
  • Save energy and prefer renewable sources.

lessons.title: Charge and Static Electricity
lessons.notes_html:
Charge is the property of matter that makes objects attract or repel each other.

Charges on Particles

  • Protons carry a positive charge.
  • Electrons carry a negative charge.
  • Neutrons carry no charge.
  • An atom is neutral because it has the same number of protons and electrons. It becomes positively charged when it loses electrons and negatively charged when it gains electrons.
  • Same charges repel each other, while opposite charges attract each other.

Static Electricity and Lightning

Charges that stay on an object give static electricity. Lightning is its major example in daily life. Lightning occurs when clouds become electrically charged by rubbing with each other and with the air around them. Clouds with huge opposite charges then collide and produce a big spark of light in the atmosphere. Current electricity, by contrast, is the flow of charges (electrons) along a wire.

Key Points

  • Protons are positive, electrons negative, neutrons neutral.
  • Like charges repel; opposite charges attract.
  • Lightning is static electricity in nature.

lessons.title: Current, Conductors and Insulators
lessons.notes_html:
Electric current is the flow of electrons along a wire. Materials differ in how well they let current pass.

Measuring Current

  • The unit used for the measurement of current is the ampere, denoted A.
  • The device used to measure current is called an ammeter.

Conductors and Insulators

  • Conductors allow current to pass through them. Example: copper, used for wires because it has high conductivity and low resistance.
  • Insulators do not allow current to pass. Example: plastic, used to cover wires for safety.

The path along which electrical current flows is called an electrical circuit.

Key Points

  • Current is the flow of electrons; its unit is the ampere.
  • An ammeter measures current.
  • Copper is a conductor; plastic is an insulator.

lessons.title: Electric Circuits and Their Parts
lessons.notes_html:
An electric circuit is the path along which current flows. A simple circuit is a closed path with four components.

Components of a Circuit

ComponentJobSymbol (in words)
Cell or batterySource of currentLong and short parallel lines, marked + and −
WireConductor that carries currentA straight line
Load (bulb, fan)Uses the currentBulb: a circle with a cross inside
SwitchGateway that opens or closes the pathA break in the wire

Open and Closed Circuits

  • Open circuit — the switch is off, the path is broken, and current cannot flow.
  • Closed circuit — the switch is on, the path is complete, and current flows through the circuit.

The brightness of a bulb is not affected by its shape; it depends on the current flowing through it.

Key Points

  • A circuit needs a source, a conductor, a load and a switch.
  • Current flows only in a closed circuit.
  • Circuit symbols are used to draw circuits neatly.

lessons.title: Series and Parallel Circuits
lessons.notes_html:
Circuits are connected in two ways: in series or in parallel.

FeatureSeries circuitParallel circuit
Paths for currentOnly one pathMore than one path
ConnectionComponents in line, one after the otherComponents connected independently, parallel to each other
CurrentSame through the whole circuitDifferent among the components
If one part failsThe entire circuit failsThe others continue to function

Uses in Daily Life

  • Series — decoration (fairy) lights, where one failed bulb darkens the whole string; battery-operated toys; smartphones.
  • Parallel — home wiring and home lighting, computer hardware, car lights (headlights, taillights, interior lights), and power grid stations distributing electricity.
  • Home wiring uses parallel circuits so that each device has its own path and keeps working if another device fails.

Key Points

  • Series has one path; parallel has many paths.
  • In series, one failure stops everything.
  • Homes are wired in parallel.

lessons.title: What Makes a Bulb Brighter?
lessons.notes_html:
The brightness of a bulb and the speed of a motor depend on how much current flows in the circuit. Several factors affect it.

Factors

  • Number of batteries — more batteries in a series circuit make the bulb glow brighter and the motor run faster.
  • Number of bulbs — more bulbs in a series circuit share the current, so each bulb becomes dimmer.
  • Type of wire — copper wires have high conductivity and low resistance, so the bulb glows brighter.
  • Length of wire — longer wires lose more power as heat, so the bulb is dimmer and the motor slower.
  • Thickness of wire — thick wires have less resistance and allow more current, so the bulb glows brighter and the motor runs faster.

The same idea works in a trip-wire security alarm: a thread holds a switch open, and when an intruder trips the thread, the switch closes, the circuit is completed, and a buzzer sounds or an LED lights.

Key Points

  • More batteries mean brighter bulbs; more bulbs in series mean dimmer bulbs.
  • Thick, short copper wires carry current best.
  • Less resistance allows more current to flow.

lessons.title: Magnets and Magnetic Materials
lessons.notes_html:
A magnet is an object that produces a magnetic field and attracts magnetic materials such as iron, nickel, cobalt and steel. Natural magnets occur as the mineral magnetite, also called lodestone.

How Magnets Were Found

The first magnet was found when the shoe nails of the Greek shepherd Magnes stuck to a rock containing magnetite.

Magnetic and Non-magnetic Materials

  • Magnetic materials are attracted by magnets: iron, nickel, cobalt and steel.
  • Non-magnetic materials are not attracted: rubber, plastic and wood.
  • Magnetism is the force of attraction or repulsion between magnets and magnetic materials.

Key Points

  • A magnet attracts iron, nickel, cobalt and steel.
  • Magnetite (lodestone) is a natural magnet.
  • Wood, plastic and rubber are non-magnetic.

lessons.title: Poles and the Magnetic Field
lessons.notes_html:
Every magnet has two poles — the North pole and the South pole — where its force is strongest and where iron filings stick the most.

Properties of Magnets

  • Attraction and repulsion — a magnet attracts magnetic materials. Like poles repel each other, while opposite (unlike) poles attract each other.
  • Pair property — if a magnet is cut into two pieces, each piece is a complete magnet with its own North and South poles.
  • Directive property — a freely moving magnet comes to rest pointing in the North–South direction.

Magnetic Field

The magnetic field is the space around a magnet in which a magnetic material feels a force of attraction or repulsion. It is shown by imaginary lines that originate from the North pole of the magnet and enter into the South pole. An electric current also produces a magnetic field: when current passes through a wire, a nearby compass needle is deflected.

Key Points

  • Like poles repel; opposite poles attract.
  • Cutting a magnet gives two complete magnets.
  • Field lines go from North pole to South pole.

lessons.title: Temporary and Permanent Magnets
lessons.notes_html:
Magnets are of three types: temporary magnets, permanent magnets and electromagnets.

FeatureTemporary magnetPermanent magnet
MagnetismKeeps magnetism only for a time; loses it easilyDoes not lose magnetism easily; poles cannot be changed
MaterialSoft metal, e.g. soft ironHard magnetic material, e.g. steel
ExampleAn iron bar magnetized by rubbing with a magnetStrong magnets used in loudspeakers

Magnetizing a Material

A magnetic material can be magnetized by stroking: rub an iron bar from one end with a bar magnet, keeping the magnet in the same position. The bar becomes magnetized and attracts small iron pieces. Electric current can also magnetize.

Demagnetizing

A magnetized material loses its magnetism by demagnetization: heating it above its Curie temperature (the temperature above which a magnet loses its magnetic properties), dropping or hammering it (mechanical stress), applying electric current, or keeping a weak magnet in the field of a strong magnet.

Key Points

  • Soft iron makes temporary magnets; hard steel makes permanent magnets.
  • Stroking with a magnet can magnetize an iron bar.
  • Heating above the Curie temperature demagnetizes a magnet.

lessons.title: Electromagnets
lessons.notes_html:
An electromagnet is a magnet in which the magnetic field is produced by an electric current.

How It Works

  • Wire is wound as a coil around an iron nail.
  • When current flows through the coil, it becomes magnetic and attracts iron nails.
  • When the switch is opened, the magnetism stops.
  • Its magnetism can be increased, reduced, stopped or produced by controlling the current, and its poles can be altered with the flow of current.
  • Its strength increases with its metal (iron) core and with the current in the coil.

Uses in Daily Life

Electromagnets are used in electric motors, generators and electric bells; in magnetic lifting in scrapyards; in MRI machines and maglev trains; in loudspeakers and microphones; and in the magnetic strips of credit and debit cards. Magnets are also used in many home appliances and devices.

Key Points

  • An electromagnet works only while current flows.
  • Its strength and poles can be controlled by the current.
  • Motors, bells, MRI machines and maglev trains use electromagnets.

lessons.title: Earth as a Magnet and the Compass
lessons.notes_html:
A freely suspended bar magnet always comes to rest pointing North–South. This happens because of its directive property: the magnet aligns itself with the Earth's magnetic field.

Earth's Poles

  • The North pole of a bar magnet corresponds to the Earth's magnetic South pole, located in the Arctic near the geographic North pole. It is called the North pole because the North pole of a compass needle points towards it.
  • The South pole of a bar magnet corresponds to the Earth's magnetic North pole, located near the coast of Antarctica.
  • The Earth's magnetic poles and geographic poles are not the same: the Earth's magnetic North pole is about 500 kilometres away from the geographic North pole.

The Compass

A compass needle orients itself towards the Earth's magnetic poles. It is a device that helps in navigation — finding direction at sea, in forests and in new places.

Key Points

  • A free magnet points North–South due to Earth's magnetic field.
  • Magnetic poles and geographic poles are different places.
  • A compass uses magnetism to navigate.

lessons.title: Science and Technology
lessons.notes_html:
Science is the knowledge obtained through observations and experiments. Scientific knowledge is not obtained through unobservance. Technology is the practical application of scientific knowledge for practical purposes.

Science vs Technology

  • Science asks and answers questions by observing and experimenting.
  • Technology uses that knowledge to make useful things and solve daily-life problems.
  • Technology has revolutionized every sphere of life — for example, in agriculture and in making useful products with microorganisms.

Horticulture

The practice of growing vegetables, fruits and flowers is called horticulture. Growing seasonal plants is an everyday use of technology in our homes and schools.

Key Points

  • Science is knowledge from observation and experiment.
  • Technology is the practical application of scientific knowledge.
  • Growing vegetables, fruits and flowers is horticulture.

lessons.title: Growing Seasonal Vegetables
lessons.notes_html:
Plants grow best in their own season. Growing seasonal plants gives us fresh food, a healthy environment, and beauty from ornamental plants.

Summer Vegetables

  • Grown in February–March and harvested in September–October (as given in the book).
  • Examples: eggplant, cucumber, okra (ladyfinger) and gourd.
  • Summer ornamental plants include marigold and daisy.

Winter Vegetables

  • Sown in September–October and harvested in February–March.
  • Examples: spinach, cabbage, turnip, onions, cauliflower, carrots, radish and garlic.
  • A winter ornamental plant named in the unit is jasmine.

Benefits of Seasonal Plants

  • They provide fresh food — fresh fruits and vegetables.
  • They make our environment healthy.
  • Ornamental plants add beauty and aesthetic value.
  • Seasonal plants are suited to their season, so they grow well with fewer inputs.

Key Points

  • Eggplant, cucumber, okra and gourd are summer vegetables.
  • Spinach, cabbage, turnip and cauliflower are winter vegetables.
  • Seasonal plants give fresh food and a healthy environment.

lessons.title: Fertilizers for Plants
lessons.notes_html:
Plants need nutrients from the soil to grow. Fertilizers supply these nutrients and increase growth and yield.

Why We Use Fertilizers

  • They supply the essential nutrients plants need for growth, such as nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.
  • They enhance soil fertility and increase plant growth and yield.

Organic and Chemical Fertilizers

  • Organic fertilizers come from animal waste, bones and plant matter, including green manure. They are rich in nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.
  • They are free from harmful chemicals and improve soil health and structure.
  • Use of organic fertilizer increases growth and yield while keeping the soil healthy.
  • In the unit's activity, pots with soil only, soil with farmyard manure and soil with chemical fertilizer are compared by germination and seedling growth.

Key Points

  • Fertilizers provide nutrients to plants.
  • Nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium are the key nutrients.
  • Organic fertilizers also improve soil health and structure.

lessons.title: Useful Microorganisms: Yogurt and Cheese
lessons.notes_html:
Beneficial microorganisms are tiny living things, like bacteria and yeast, that are useful to mankind. They convert milk into yogurt and cheese by fermentation. Milk products include yogurt, cheese, butter and cream.

Making Yogurt at Home

  • Take about one litre of raw milk and heat it with stirring to 82°C.
  • Let it cool to around 45°C.
  • Add a spoonful of yogurt starter culture (containing beneficial bacteria) and stir thoroughly.
  • Keep it in a warm place at about 38–40°C for 10–12 hours, then chill it in the refrigerator. The yogurt is ready.

Making Cheese at Home

  • Materials: 1 litre milk, 1 tablespoon lemon juice, white (distilled) vinegar, salt, cheesecloth and rennet (an enzyme).
  • Heat the milk at 63°C for 30 minutes to kill harmful bacteria; cool to around 32°C.
  • Add lemon juice or vinegar and stir; let it incubate for an hour so the acid curdles the milk.
  • Add rennet to coagulate the curds. When the whey separates from the curd, add salt, transfer the curds to cheesecloth and shape the cheese.

Key Points

  • Starter culture bacteria ferment milk into yogurt.
  • Rennet is the enzyme used to make cheese.
  • Cheese-making separates whey from curd.

lessons.title: Solar Oven and Electric Bell
lessons.notes_html:
Technology also works in the kitchen and at the door. Both devices in this lesson change one form of energy into another.

The Solar Oven

  • Materials: a cardboard box, aluminum foil, plastic wrap, scissors, dark paper, pencil, glue or tape.
  • Cut a flap in the top of the box as a lid; cover the inside with aluminum foil; cover the bottom with black construction paper.
  • Place a small pot in the centre, close the lid with plastic wrap tight, and cut a small hole in the lid for ventilation.
  • Working: the oven converts solar radiation into heat energy. The foil reflects light onto the pot, the dark paper absorbs heat, and the plastic wrap traps heat inside to cook the food.

The Electric Bell

  • Its main part is an electromagnet: a U-shaped iron piece wound with wire, a soft iron strip (armature) with a hammer, a gong, a battery, a switch and a screw.
  • When the button is pushed, current flows, the electromagnet attracts the strip, and the hammer strikes the gong.
  • The strip then leaves the screw, the circuit breaks, the electromagnet demagnetizes, and the strip returns. This repeats, so the bell keeps ringing until the button is released.

Key Points

  • A solar oven changes solar radiation into heat.
  • Dark surfaces absorb heat; foil reflects light; plastic wrap traps heat.
  • An electric bell rings with the help of an electromagnet.

lessons.title: The Solar System and the Sun
lessons.notes_html:
The solar system is the part of the Milky Way galaxy that includes the Sun and everything revolving around it: the eight planets, comets, asteroids, meteorites and satellites. The Sun is at the centre of the solar system.

The Sun — Our Star

  • A star is a celestial body that emits its own light and energy due to nuclear reactions inside it. The Sun is a star.
  • The Sun is a medium-sized star — a huge ball of hot, glowing gases, about 75% hydrogen and 25% helium by mass.
  • It emits heat and light continuously and is the only source of heat, light and energy for all the planets.
  • The eight planets revolve around the Sun at different distances. The Earth revolves anticlockwise around the Sun at about 109,000 km per hour.

Key Points

  • Our solar system is part of the Milky Way galaxy.
  • The Sun is composed of hydrogen and helium.
  • The Sun is the centre and the only energy source of the solar system.

lessons.title: The Eight Planets in Order
lessons.notes_html:
There are 8 planets in our solar system. In order from the Sun, they are: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

Planets Near the Sun

  • Mercury — the closest planet to the Sun and the smallest planet, with a diameter of about 4879 km. It has a rocky surface and no atmosphere, no water is found on it, and it becomes extremely hot during the day and cold at night.
  • Venus — the hottest planet of the solar system.
  • Earth — the only planet on which life exists. Its natural satellite is the Moon.
  • Mars — called the red planet due to its red colour. It has an atmosphere and a rocky surface and has frozen water; scientists are exploring it by sending space missions.

The Far Planets

Jupiter, Saturn and Uranus follow Mars, and Neptune is the eighth, last and farthest planet from the Sun. A planet has no light of its own; it shines by the Sun's light and revolves around the Sun.

Key Points

  • Mercury is closest and smallest; Neptune is farthest.
  • Venus is the hottest planet; Mars is the red planet.
  • Life exists only on Earth.

lessons.title: Stars, Planets and Dwarf Planets
lessons.notes_html:
The solar system contains different kinds of celestial bodies. Knowing how they differ makes the sky easy to understand.

FeatureStarPlanet
Own lightEmits its own light and energy (nuclear reactions inside)Has no light or energy of its own
MovementStays at the centre of its systemRevolves around the Sun (a star)
ExampleThe SunEarth, Mars, Jupiter

Dwarf Planets

Smaller bodies that revolve around the Sun are called dwarf planets. Five dwarf planets are officially recognized: Pluto, Eris, Ceres, Haumea and Makemake. Pluto is the dwarf planet named most often in this unit.

Key Points

  • Stars make their own light; planets do not.
  • Pluto, Eris, Ceres, Haumea and Makemake are dwarf planets.
  • Planets revolve around the Sun.

lessons.title: Asteroids, Meteorites and Comets
lessons.notes_html:
Besides planets, many rocky and icy bodies move around the Sun.

Asteroids

  • An asteroid is a piece of rock that revolves around the Sun.
  • Asteroids are found between Mars and Jupiter, where they form a belt called the asteroid belt.
  • They vary in size — some are small and some are as large as dwarf planets — and they have no atmosphere.

Meteorites

Meteorites are rocks from outer space, formed by the collision of asteroids, that fall on a moon or a planet. They are usually small and light. Entering the atmosphere, a meteorite becomes a meteor — a fireball or shooting star.

Comets

  • A comet is a combination of dust, rock and ice that orbits the Sun in an elliptical orbit.
  • When it comes near the Sun, the dust and gases burn and spew up, forming a glowing head and tail.
  • Halley's Comet is the most well-known comet, named after Edmond Halley, who first predicted its return in 1758.
  • It is made of ice, dust and rocky particles, can be seen with the naked eye every 75–76 years, was last seen in 1986, and will return again in 2061.

Key Points

  • The asteroid belt lies between Mars and Jupiter.
  • A meteor is seen as a fireball or shooting star.
  • Halley's Comet returns every 76 years; next in 2061.

lessons.title: Satellites: Natural and Artificial
lessons.notes_html:
A satellite is an object that revolves around a planet in a specified orbit. Satellites are of two types.

Natural Satellites

Natural satellites are celestial bodies that revolve around a planet and do not have their own light. The moons of the planets are natural satellites — for example, the Moon is the natural satellite of Earth. Sputnik was the first artificial satellite.

Artificial Satellites

  • Geostationary satellites — 35,800 km above the equator, moving west to east with the Earth, so they appear stationary. Used for telecommunication, broadcasting and navigation.
  • Weather satellites — in low polar orbit. They scan the Earth for meteorological conditions and help in weather forecasting.
  • Communication satellites — in geostationary orbit. They transmit radio, TV and mobile phone signals.
  • GPS satellites — more than 30 orbiting the Earth. They tell the position of something or someone on Earth; GPS is used for navigation.

Artificial satellites have greatly improved our knowledge of space by observing the Earth continuously from space.

Key Points

  • The Moon is a natural satellite; Sputnik was the first artificial one.
  • Geostationary satellites appear stationary at 35,800 km.
  • GPS satellites give exact positions for navigation.
